strongest_objection: The map's own boundary claim excludes the bribe because 'no power moves, only an outcome', and one member fails that test as written. Silence on the tab has the reporter give 'the power to publish, one item at a time' for access, with silence 'bought again at every story': that is access paid for one non-exercise at a time, the bribe shape with access as the currency. The item survives only because of the ratchet it describes, and the ratchet is the power transfer the text never names: every story withheld is sunk into the relationship, so the source accumulates a standing veto over the reporter that is never renegotiated and grows without being re-granted. Naming that veto as what passes, and the sunk stories as its carrier, makes the item type-compliant and stranger, not tamer. The second objection is at the itinerary's far endpoint: Key man's lever says the minted lever sits in 'a hand that did not sit at the table', but the named partner is usually the firm's own voice at that table; the true mechanism is that the trade arms a member of one side against its own side, which the text should say. I tried to collapse Veto sold as an improbability into Drag for tag (both price a power over a future state at signing and pay at certainty) and could not: a founder who knows the base rate perfectly still gives a drag for a tag and the drag still governs, so the two run on different asymmetries.

items.item: Silence on the tab: a reporter or an analyst gives the power to publish, one item at a time, and receives access; the carrier is the repeated game, since access is revocable at any moment and silence must be bought again at every story; the rate ratchets, because each story withheld is an investment in the relationship that a disclosure would forfeit, so the price of the next disclosure rises with every one not made; found one-sided when the access yields only what cannot be printed and the power to publish has quietly become a power to know; not discretion sold as a good, a single sale, but a lease whose rent rises with the tenancy.
items.why: As written it is a per-story fee for a non-exercise and fails the map's own bribe exclusion ('no power moves, only an outcome'). The mechanism that rescues it, the ratchet, is a standing power the source holds and the text never names. The repair names the veto that passes and its carrier (the reporter's own sunk stories), keeps the ratchet, and fixes 'rent rises with the tenancy', which misplaces the ratchet: the source's rent stays flat, and it is the reporter's cost of breaking the lease that climbs.
items.repair: Silence on the tab: a reporter or an analyst gives a source a veto over each story in exchange for access, and the veto outlives the story, since access is revocable at any moment and every story withheld is an investment in the relationship that the next disclosure would forfeit; the carrier is the repeated game and the reporter's own sunk stories, not any one item, so the source holds a standing power to make the reporter refrain that grows without ever being re-granted; the rate ratchets, because the price of the next disclosure rises with every one not made while the rent the source pays stays flat; found one-sided when the access yields only what cannot be printed and the power to publish has quietly become a power to know; not a bribe, an outcome bought once and priced fresh each time, since here the hold accumulates in what the reporter has already withheld, and not discretion sold as a good, a single sale, but a lease whose breaking fee rises with the tenancy.

items.item: Hostage returned as partisan: two parties each give the other a power to punish them through a body they value, as in the medieval exchange of sons and the hostages Rome took from client kings, and each receives the same hold over the other; the carrier is the body together with the giver's continuing love for it, since a hostage the giver stops valuing holds nothing, so the rate is the ratio of the two givers' caring and not the ranks of the persons exchanged; the trade inverts, on the standard reading of Roman practice, when the hostage raised in the holder's house returns as its friend, so the giver gave a hold and got back a party of the other side; not the ugly hostage of who-can-be-bound, a token worth nothing to its holder and posted one way, since this hold is mutual and its product changes sides.
items.why: The item defines the trade as mutual ('two parties each give the other', 'each receives the same hold') and then rests its inversion on Roman practice, which was one-way: Rome took hostages from client kings and gave none, and what the king received was confirmation on his throne. The discriminator against who-can-be-bound's Ugly hostage is built on that mutuality, so the item's main case fails its own discriminator. The real difference from the ugly hostage is not mutuality but that the holder comes to value the body too, which is exactly what lets it be turned; the repair says so and keeps the inversion, the standard-reading modality, and the caring-ratio rate.
items.repair: Hostage returned as partisan: a party gives another a power to punish it through a body it values, and receives a hold or a confirmation back, as in the medieval exchange of sons between truce-makers, which ran both ways, and the hostages Rome took from client kings, which ran one way and paid in the king's throne; the carrier is the body together with the giver's continuing love for it, since a hostage the giver stops valuing holds nothing, so the rate is set by the givers' caring and not by the ranks of the persons given; the trade inverts, on the standard reading of Roman practice, when the hostage raised in the holder's house returns as its friend, so the giver gave a hold and got back a party of the other side; not the ugly hostage of who-can-be-bound, a token worth nothing to its holder, since here the holder comes to value the body too, and that is what lets it be turned.

items.item: Customs house: a state gives foreign creditors the power to collect its customs and receives a loan, as the Ottoman Public Debt Administration from 1881 and the Dominican receivership of 1905 put creditors' clerks at the revenue's source; the carrier is the receivership itself, an occupation of the place where the money enters; the rate is set by the lender's model of default and not by what the state thinks its sovereignty is worth, so the power is priced as a yield; the loan has a maturity and the receivership has none, so the power returns only by an act of expulsion the carrier never wrote, which the debtor must some decade find the strength to perform; not conditionality, which binds by the next tranche and can be dropped by dropping the tranche.
items.why: 'Returns only by an act of expulsion' is an illustrative case asserted as history that the item's own named cases contradict: the Ottoman Administration lost its writ in Turkey by the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 and the Dominican receivership closed by the Trujillo-Hull treaty of 1940, both negotiated, the second bought with a new pledge of the same revenue. The mechanism (the loan matures and the occupation does not, so return needs an act outside the carrier) is right and is kept; the act is a war, a repudiation, or a new treaty, not expulsion.
items.repair: Customs house: a state gives foreign creditors the power to collect its customs and receives a loan, as the Ottoman Public Debt Administration from 1881 and the Dominican receivership of 1905 put creditors' clerks at the revenue's source; the carrier is the receivership itself, an occupation of the place where the money enters; the rate is set by the lender's model of default and not by what the state thinks its sovereignty is worth, so the power is priced as a yield; the loan has a maturity and the receivership has none, so the power returns only by an act the carrier never wrote, a war, a repudiation, or a new treaty bought with a new pledge, as Lausanne in 1923 and the Trujillo-Hull treaty of 1940 did, which the debtor must some decade find the strength or the credit to perform; not conditionality, which binds by the next tranche and can be dropped by dropping the tranche.

items.item: Key man's lever: investors in a fund give their commitment and receive the power to suspend the fund's investing if named partners leave; the carrier is the limited partnership agreement; the rate looks cheap to the firm, which does not plan to lose the named, but the trade mints a power in a hand that did not sit at the table, since each named partner now holds a lever over its own firm, leaving triggers the suspension, and can price its staying at every renegotiation; the firm's power over its own partners is what was quietly sold; found one-sided when a named partner asks for more carry with the agreement open on the table; not a hostage, who is held, since the key man holds.
items.why: 'A hand that did not sit at the table' is false in the common case: the named partners are usually the firm's own negotiators of the limited partnership agreement. They are not a party to it, which is the claim the endpoint needs, and the stranger fact is that the firm's own voice at the table walks away holding a lever against the firm. The repair says both and leaves the rest untouched, so the seriation endpoint 'a hand that never sat at the table' should read 'a hand that was never a party'.
items.repair: Key man's lever: investors in a fund give their commitment and receive the power to suspend the fund's investing if named partners leave; the carrier is the limited partnership agreement; the rate looks cheap to the firm, which does not plan to lose the named, but the trade mints a power in a hand that was never a party to it and was often the firm's own voice at the table, since each named partner now holds a lever over its own firm, leaving triggers the suspension, and can price its staying at every renegotiation; the firm's power over its own partners is what was quietly sold; found one-sided when a named partner asks for more carry with the agreement open on the table; not a hostage, who is held, since the key man holds.

items.item: Veto sold as an improbability: a founder gives an investor class consent rights over named future states, a sale below a price, a new financing, a change to the charter, and receives a higher valuation now; the carrier is the charter's protective provisions, held by class vote; the rate is set by the founder's estimate of how unlikely those states are, so the veto is sold at the price of an improbability and exercised at the price of a certainty, and the buyer, who has seen a hundred companies reach those states, knows the base rate better than the seller who has seen one; found one-sided the day the improbable arrives and the acqui-hire that would save the team needs a signature from a class that would receive nothing; not control, since a veto can keep a future from happening and cannot make one happen.
items.why: Tested as the left of my closest pair; survives (see neighbor_test).

items.item: Drag for tag: a minority gives the majority the power to force its shares into a sale and receives the right to join any sale the majority makes; the carrier is the shareholders' agreement; the rate is symmetric in the text and asymmetric in frequency, since drags fire at nearly every exit and tags almost never, because majorities rarely sell in part, so a swap of two powers over two futures is priced as if the futures were equally likely and pays out as if only one existed; found one-sided when the drag fires at a price the majority's preference makes handsome and the minority's common makes nothing. Adds to impasse-inventions' swap of vetoes the shape of the rate: a power-for-power swap is priced by which future arrives, not by the powers' text.
items.why: Tested as the right of my closest pair; survives. One overstatement noted under modality: drags are invoked rarely and govern nearly every exit as the threat under which holdouts sign; the frequency asymmetry the item needs holds either way.

neighbor_test.separating_case: Both price a power over a future state at signing by an estimate and pay it out at certainty, so they are the pair most tempting to collapse into 'a power priced as a probability'. Case: a founder on her fourth company who knows the base rates as well as the investor gives a drag and takes a tag. The veto's mechanism dies for her, since with the base-rate gap closed the consent right is priced at what it costs and nothing is found one-sided. The drag's does not: the drag still governs every exit and the tag still almost never fires, because that asymmetry is in how often the two futures arrive and no information cures it; the carrier is the customary pairing that presents the two as a matched set. Converse: an investor who buys a veto over a state both sides agree is likely (a down round in a bad market) is a Veto trade with no improbability in it and no collision with any drag. So Veto sold as an improbability is an information asymmetry in a power-for-money sale, and Drag for tag is a frequency asymmetry in a power-for-power swap; a party can be cured of one and not the other. They do not collapse.

boundary_case: The hired agent: a client gives counsel a power of attorney, or a fund gives a proxy advisor its ballot, and receives service. It has a power given, a thing received, a carrier (the instrument), and a rate (the fee), so the declared type admits it on its face. Ruling: out, and the ruling sharpens the type. In ordinary agency the power keeps its address: the courts, the registry, and every third party still route to the principal, the agent exercises the power for the principal's account, and the principal pays rather than receives. Every member of this map has the carrier re-address the power, so third parties route to the taker and the taker exercises it for its own account: the proxy card re-addresses the vote for one meeting to an activist with its own interest, the registry re-addresses the summons to the nominee, the charter's protective provisions re-address the consent to a class. The test the map should state is 'does the carrier change where the power is found and for whose account it is exercised', and the map's own boundary claim about the bribe is the same test from the other side: the bribe changes neither. Blame-bearer's fee is the instructive middle, an agency that is in only because the registry moves the address, and it should say so.

seriation.note: Endpoints are real: a vote lent by card and returned by the clock with nothing worn off, and a power that did not exist before the trade. The itinerary is declared as authored and the consequential adjacency Seat for the check → Fence around the process teaches an operator test (is the carrier the power or a pointer to it) that nothing in the bare pile states. The hinge Sword → Queen → Kingmaker gives three routes of consumption and is the map's best stretch. Two notes. The axis sentence omits the 'returns transformed by a third party' station (Hostage, Name on the door, Blame-bearer's fee) that the note describes and the edges use; the axis should name it between 'bought again at every turn' and 'cannot be passed on'. And the far endpoint's wording, 'a hand that never sat at the table', should become 'a hand that was never a party' after the Key man repair; the itinerary is unchanged. Vote that dies in transit sitting between the transformed group and the consumed group is defensible (a power consumed on transfer is the doorway to powers consumed in the giving) but is the one adjacency that teaches least; no reorder is argued.

edges.why: The incompatibility is real but the label's antecedent cannot fail as stated, because in standard venture paper the drag trigger and the sale veto sit in the same preferred majority, which would not drag a sale it vetoes; the collision only exists when the two powers sit in different hands. Naming that condition makes the label a claim with a failure case and names where an operator should look: a stacked syndicate with series-level protective provisions.
edges.repair_label: If the drag and the veto sit in different hands, as when a senior series triggers the drag on a sale at its own preference and a junior series holding its own protective provisions would receive nothing, the drag cannot fire without a signature that has no reason to come, so two powers each sold as an improbability collide in the same improbable state and only one can hold; standard paper hides the collision by lodging both powers in one preferred majority, and a stacked syndicate brings it back.

edges.why: The dependency holds only where the charter counts a proxy grant as a transfer, which most transfer sunsets do, with an exception for cards the board itself solicits. The item Vote that dies in transit speaks only of shares leaving the founder's hands, so the label silently extends the conversion to proxies; stating the condition makes the antecedent failable and tells the reader which clause to check.
edges.repair_label: If the charter counts a proxy to an outsider as a transfer, as transfer sunsets commonly do with an exception for cards the board itself solicits, an activist can borrow from every holder except the founder, whose high vote dies when it moves; the proxy market exists only among votes that survive transfer, so the trade at the head of the itinerary is barred from the one holder with the most to lend.

edges.why: Consequential on the Hostage repair: the trade is no longer defined as mutual, and the passage runs the same for the one-way Roman hostage, who is valued by the holder that raised him and by the father who sent him.
edges.repair_label: If the giver goes on valuing the hostage, the hostage holds a lever of its own over the giver, and one raised to be the holder's friend holds one over both, so a hostage trade mints in the body exchanged the power the key-man clause mints in the named partner; the passage from inverted to minted runs through a person who learns it is valued by both sides.

edges.from_handle: First look that chills the room
edges.why: Tested: the antecedent fails if the first look is waived or the insider declines to lead; the loop with the previous edge is real, and it runs through price rather than through the fence lapsing, since the insider inside a free fence retrades in the last week instead of letting it go cold. A bare sequence shows two exclusivity clauses; only the pair of edges shows the ratchet.

modality_problems: Hostage returned as partisan: defines the trade as mutual and rests the inversion on Roman hostage-taking, which was one-way (repaired).
Customs house: 'returns only by an act of expulsion' contradicted by the item's own cases, both of which ended by treaty, Lausanne 1923 and Trujillo-Hull 1940 (repaired).
Key man's lever: 'a hand that did not sit at the table' is false in the common case where the named partners negotiate the agreement; the defensible claim is 'not a party' (repaired).

Silence on the tab: 'gives the power to publish, one item at a time' describes a per-outcome fee, which the map's own boundary claim excludes; the standing veto that makes it a trade was unnamed (repaired).

Drag for tag: 'drags fire at nearly every exit' overstates; drags are invoked rarely and govern nearly every exit as the threat under which holdouts sign. The frequency asymmetry survives the correction, so no repair.

Card for one meeting: 'the activist settles with the board for two seats before the vote' is stated as the standard unwinding; it is the common one but the map should not be read as saying proxy fights usually settle. Left as is.
duplication: none at the level of the map; no grown list has a power passing between parties as its item type. Item-level adjacencies the record already names: Leased strike to ghost-leverages (the automated plant's strike threat), Drag for tag and First look to impasse-inventions (swap of vetoes, right of first refusal), Hostage to who-can-be-bound (Ugly hostage), Name on the door to status-conversions. One adjacency the record does not name and should: Blame-bearer's fee shares its carrier with who-can-be-bound's Rented door (a summons goes where the registry points); it adds that the liability follows the summons to the nominee instead of counting as received by the principal. Within this run, not grown: Vote that dies in transit sits next to dilution-carriers' Ten votes a share, and Veto sold as an improbability next to term-sheet-powers' Veto priced by the clock and dilution-carriers' Veto without votes; the three veto items are three mechanisms (price at signing, value at the moment of exercise, class vote without votes) and can coexist, but the fleet editor should see them side by side.
best_unresolved_seed: The closing condition that mints hold-up power in a true stranger. A buyer and a seller agree that the close needs a landlord's consent to assign the lease, a customer's consent to change of control, or a named engineer's signed retention agreement, and the trade between two parties creates in a third, who never sat at the table and was never a party, the power to stop it and to price not stopping it. That is the literal endpoint the map's itinerary names and Key man's lever only approximates from inside one side; it also answers the ledger's crossfield question (which trades create a party rather than move a power) with a case where the two who minted the power cannot buy it back without the third's consent. The ledger's rejected residue 'Hand that cannot close' is the same seed seen from the privilege's side.
independent_review_line: Fable critic: admitted after repairing four items (Silence on the tab, which as written was a per-story fee the map's own bribe exclusion bars, now naming the source's accumulating veto; Hostage returned as partisan, whose mutual definition its Roman case contradicts; Customs house, whose 'expulsion' both named receiverships refute; Key man's lever, whose named partner sat at the table as the firm and is repaired to 'never a party') and sharpening two edge labels whose antecedents could not fail as written, after failing to collapse Veto sold as an improbability into Drag for tag.
